guide.intro: Google DSA roadmap, research-updated Sept 2026. For 5–6 focused hours/day, first interviews month 3–4, ~3–4/10 on unseen mediums. Built from LeetCode Discuss candidate reports (2024–2026), topic-frequency analysis across ~600 reported Google problems, and Google's 2026 process changes. ~200 new problems on purpose — candidates who cleared report 150–250 with deep understanding, not 500+ shallow.

research.title: There's a gate before the interviews: the GHA
research.text: The Google Hiring Assessment is a pass/fail behavioural screen that arrives 24–72 h after applying — 50–75 Likert statements, 30 minutes, one sitting, no back button, ~4–5 day deadline, reported six-month reapply window. It measures integrity, collaboration, ownership, ambiguity-handling and communication, and cross-checks consistency. Handle it in week 0.

research.title: Google problems come wrapped in ambiguity
research.text: The most consistent 2025–2026 theme isn't difficulty — it's deliberately vague framing. "Parse a chat log and return the K most talkative users", "a network of teleporters, some broken, return the path". Underneath: top-K heap, BFS, DP. The algorithm is standard; the statement is not. Nobody practises this, and it's why strong LeetCode solvers fail Google specifically.

research.title: The 2026 process has changed
research.text: In-person rounds are back at many locations. AI is banned in standard loops (policy varies by round — confirm with your recruiter). A code-comprehension round is piloting (read and debug an unfamiliar 200–500 line codebase in CoderPad). L3 has no system design round; L4 sometimes chooses three coding rounds.

research.title: Topic frequency decides where hours go
research.text: Arrays + Trees + DP + Graphs ≈ 63% of ~600 reported problems; those four are weeks 1–9. Google has the highest hard share in FAANG (~19%), and graph problems are displacing pure string problems in 2026 OA rounds.

research.title: On the Premium Google tag
research.text: Contested value. Use the Discuss interview-experience compilations instead — one L3 offer-holder compiled every Google question from 2022–2024 posts and hit three verbatim in his loop. If you buy Premium, one month for weeks 9–14 only.

rules: No editorial before 25 minutes. Not a hint, not a tag, not an LLM.
Every problem is re-solved at +3 and +14 days, from a blank file. This converts exposure into retrieval and is the direct fix for 3–4/10.
After the editorial: close it, re-implement from scratch.
Tagged practice is fine in Phase 1. Untagged from Phase 2, except the weekly measurement set which is untagged from week 1.
20% of all practice happens in a blank Google Doc or on paper. No IDE, no autocomplete, no execution. With in-person rounds back, add whiteboard or paper sessions from week 9.

dailyTemplate.content: 3 new problems (2 on hard days and all of weeks 6–7). 25-min hard timer → 5 min writing what you know and which constraint you haven't used → editorial → close → re-implement blank.
The day's +3 and +14 queue. Even on bad days. Short on time? Cut Block A, never Block B.
Editorials incl. alternate approaches · trigger notes · triage drill (15 min) · one variant, mandatory.
Blind primitives — pick 5 (daily, 20 min) + rotation: Tue debug hunt · Wed code quality · Thu ambiguity drill · Fri code comprehension · Sat cold-combo.

dailyNotes: Weekly shape: 5 full days + 1 contest half-day + 1 full rest day.
Contest day (3h): 90-min LeetCode weekly or biweekly, 90-min post-mortem solving everything missed, untimed. Then stop.

phase2Template.content: 2 problems, random and untagged, 40/60 medium/hard, spoken aloud, recorded, 2 variants each, half of them posed as ambiguous scenarios.

drills.name: Spaced re-solve
drills.text: 12-minute timebox. Can't finish → failure → re-queue +3/+14 from today. Clean pass at +14 → retire. Failed twice → add +30. Passing means you reconstructed the reasoning, not recalled the code — typed something memorised and can't state the invariant out loud? Fail, even if it submits green.

drills.name: Ambiguity drill
drills.text: Take a solved problem and rewrite it as a vague real-world scenario the way a Google interviewer would pose it. Come back to it a week later (or have a friend read it cold) and practise the derivation out loud: clarifying questions, stated assumptions, explicit edge cases. Source scenarios from Discuss Google interview-experience posts.

drills.name: Variant generation
drills.text: After solving anything, pick one variant and solve it. Reported Google rounds routinely include 2–3 follow-ups after the initial solve — this drill is the second half of every round.

drills.name: Triage
drills.text: Ten problems you will not solve, 90 seconds each: constraints suggest · trigger phrase · pattern guess · why not greedy. Then check tags. Ten pattern-recognition reps at a tenth the cost of solving ten.

drills.name: Blind primitives
drills.text: 2 you failed most recently (from the bug log) · 2 you haven't touched in a week · 1 from this week's topic. Instantiate, don't stub. Verify every attempt by pasting into a real problem. Retire nothing, but taper: clean four times running → monthly spot-check.

drills.name: Debug hunt
drills.text: Break a solved problem deliberately (off-by-one, flipped comparison, missing base case, answer recorded before the shrink). Wait a day. Find it by hand-tracing a small input — no execution. Exactly what a shared-doc round demands.

drills.name: Code quality pass
drills.text: Rewrite two of the week's solutions as if for code review: descriptive names, extracted helpers, guard clauses, no magic numbers. Could an interviewer follow this while you narrate? Google grades readability explicitly.

drills.name: Code comprehension
drills.text: Open an unfamiliar 200–500 line file from a real open-source repo, ideally a language you don't write daily. Out loud: what does it do in two sentences · inputs, outputs, invariants · where would a bug hide · complexity of the hot path · what would you change. This is the pilot round's exact shape.

drills.name: Cold-combo
drills.text: Write a primitive inside an actual problem under time pressure, rather than in isolation. The check against a skeleton becoming its own memorised artifact.

guide.bugLog: Every failed primitive attempt gets one line, e.g. "Dijkstra — forgot to skip stale PQ entries on pop". This selects your first two primitives each day; after a month it maps your personal bug fingerprint. Keep it in Notes.

guide.primitivesGoal: Blank file, zero reference, timed. 22 primitives; targets are fluency targets, not learning targets. Daily: pick 5 — 2 you failed most recently, 2 untouched for a week, 1 from this week's topic. #9, #18 and #21 carry path reconstruction deliberately: "return the actual sequence, not the value" is one of Google's most common follow-ups.

Return the actual sequence/path, not just its length/value

trigger phrase: "minimum number of X such that..."

verbalProtocol: Restate the problem in your own words. Confirm.

Ask 2–3 clarifying questions and state your assumptions explicitly — with Google's ambiguous framing this is scored. Input size? Duplicates? Ties? Who parses the input? Fits in memory? Return the value or the actual path?
State a brute force and its complexity. Skipping this reads as pattern-matching.
Propose the optimisation and its complexity before coding.
Code, narrating. Clean names — readability is graded.
Dry-run a small example by hand, out loud. No execution available.
Volunteer your own test cases — interviewers ask candidates to enumerate test scenarios unprompted.
State time and space complexity, justified. Offer a follow-up improvement.
googleyness: Disagreeing with a senior engineer's technical decision (reported 2026 prompt)
A project you drove without authority
exitCriteria: Unseen medium: pattern in ≤5 min, solved in ≤25, bug-free first submission, ~80% of the time.
Unseen hard: solved in 40–45 min about half the time.
Ambiguous scenario → correct specification in ≤5 min of clarifying questions.
Two follow-up variants handled on the spot without restarting.
From memory in under 8 min: Dijkstra · Union-Find · both topological sorts · LIS O(n log n) · trie · quickselect · two-heaps median · edit distance grid.
New DP problem: state / transition / base / order correct before any code.
Time and space stated and justified unprompted, every time.
Ten Googleyness stories written and rehearsed; GHA completed.
failureModes: Failing the GHA before you ever code. Handle it in week 0.
Skipping Block B. Revision feels unproductive because you're re-solving things you "already know." You don't.
Practising only clean problem statements. Google's ambiguity is intentional; the Thursday drill exists for this.
Skipping variants. At Google that's skipping half of every round.
Jumping straight to optimal. Reads as memorisation. State the brute force.
Practising only mediums. Google has the highest hard share in FAANG.
Only practising in an IDE. Shared doc, no autocomplete, no execution — and in-person rounds mean paper too.
Skipping the rest day. A burnout crash costs two weeks you don't have.
recruiter: In-person or remote? Determines paper vs shared-doc practice.
Does my loop include the code-comprehension round? If yes, weight the Friday drill heavily.
Is AI permitted in any round? Policy is per-round now. Assume banned unless you have it in writing.

guide.scope: L3 has no system design round. L4 sometimes chooses three coding rounds over two coding + one design. Targeting L3/L4, the only non-DSA prep is the GHA and the Googleyness round. L5+ needs a separate system design track. Process details reflect reporting as of September 2026 — re-check before your loop.

weeks.title: Week 0 — GHA & diagnostic

items.name: Read Google's published values and the "Googleyness" language
Write your genuine positions: owning a mistake under pressure · disagreeing with a senior engineer · ambiguous requirements · sharing credit · escalating vs resolving · handling sensitive data
Decide: answer decisively and consistently, as yourself. Block a quiet 60 min when the invite arrives — no pause, no back button

Classify each failure: didn't see the pattern → triage 15/day · saw it, couldn't code → primitives daily · bugs → weekly debug hunt + dry-run habit · too slow → tighter timers, both contests
Record the score in Notes — weeks 4, 8 and 11 measure against it

notes: The GHA is a pass/fail behavioural screen that arrives 24–72 h after applying: 50–75 Likert statements, 30 minutes, one sitting, ~4–5 day deadline, reported six-month reapply window. You could do 400 hours of DSA and never reach a coding round. Handle it now.
It rewards defensible, decisive choices and cross-checks consistency across rephrased items. Answer as yourself, consistently — not as an imagined ideal candidate.

notes: Flagged problems are verified high-frequency in Google reports. Max Path Sum and Validate BST both appear repeatedly; Max Path Sum was identified as the basis of an actual Google India OA problem.

The pattern that matters most: post-order aggregate — recurse into children, get a tuple from each, combine at the node, return a possibly-different tuple upward while updating a global. Diameter, Max Path Sum, Balanced, House Robber III and Longest Univalue Path are the same algorithm in different clothes.
The recurring subtlety: what you return upward is often not what you record as the answer.
Block D aligned slot this week: post-order tree shell and iterative inorder.

notes: DP is 15% of reported problems and the only topic classified Hard across the board. Two weeks, two problems a day, done properly.

Non-negotiable format before any code: state (dp[i] = precise English meaning) · transition · base · order. Then recursive + memo → tabulation → space optimisation. Full chain on the first problem of each new sub-pattern only.
Coin Change vs Coin Change II differ only in loop order, and that difference is combinations vs permutations.
On LIS: also write the reconstruction. Returning the subsequence rather than its length is a standard follow-up.
